details:
From Age Verification FAQ:

"Persona keeps your data to prevent the usage of the same ID for multiple accounts."

This sounds completely unnecessary. I may be oversimplifying, but can't they just take the id data (name, birthday, country, etc) and compute a hash? They could then delete the id data and store the hash. If someone tried to use the same id data inputs again, they would produce the same hash, so Persona can prevent using the same id multiple times without storing any of the id's actual information.

This is similar to a database storing hashed passwords instead of plain-text passwords. No sensitive information is stored.

The "tricky" part of this solution is deciding on the standardized set of id data to hash on. You need sufficient data to make a person unique (two people with same name, same birthday, same country, etc is an edge case to consider, a "natural duplicate"). The id data input is ideally information that everyone has (not everyone has a driver's license number). There could also be additional steps in place that occur when a user tries to verify using input data that hashes to an existing hash. For example, you could track the number of times a hash is used and introduce timeouts / throttling. You could request additional id data when someone tries to verify using an existing hash. There are many ways to create a system like this to combat multiple account creation. You might not be able to 100% prevent multiple accounts while still allowing natural duplicates to create accounts (two real people with same id data are natural duplicates), but you could certainly make it much more difficult and time consuming to create multiple accounts. Alternatively, if the id data set was sufficient enough to provide uniqueness, then you would essentially eliminate the occurrences of natural duplicates and could prevent multiple account creation.

Anyway, I'm sure they can figure out a decent set of id data to hash on that provides sufficient uniqueness, and the appropriate steps to take when a duplicate hash is reached. This solution may not be perfect, but it sounds a lot better than storing personal information and it still provides some protection against multiple accounts. If the current plan allows people to simply delete their stored data and then create multiple accounts, then there wasn't really much protection against multiple accounts in the first place.
title: Why not hash the id data?
